query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the traditional EAM reference potentials with deep neural network (DNN)–based interatomic potentials trained on a diverse set of ab initio liquid configurations will improve the phase‐space overlap between the reference and ab initio target, thus reducing the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys, in both solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures.
generation.intervention: Substitute the EAM-based reference with a deep neural network potential that has been trained on a wide array of atomic configurations obtained from ab initio simulations of the liquid state.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applicable near and at the high melting temperature range (e.g., above ~3000 K for refractory high-entropy alloys) and at compositions typical of high-entropy systems (near equiatomic ratios).
generation.structural_mediator: The DNN potential, by being trained on a comprehensive dataset, more accurately reproduces the local atomic arrangements and pair correlations characteristic of the liquid state than the limited EAM approach.
generation.mechanism: By capturing many-body and subtle interatomic effects absent in EAM formulations, the DNN potential improves the overlap between the configuration spaces of the reference and target (ab initio liquid). This enhanced phase-space overlap should reduce the integration path length and mismatch encountered during thermodynamic integration.
generation.predicted_outcome: A pronounced reduction (potentially on the order of magnitude improvement, although an exact factor is uncertain) in the thermodynamic integration mismatch relative to using TOR-TILD's EAM references, leading to more accurate free-energy estimates.
generation.baseline: Traditional thermodynamic integration using EAM reference potentials as employed in TOR-TILD.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements may be confined to high-temperature regimes and specific compositions of high-entropy alloys with refractory or similar characteristics; the approach might not translate to materials with very different bonding or lower melting point systems.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the reduction in integration path mismatch is not yet quantified. Variability across different alloy compositions and temperatures could affect the level of improvement, and further systematic testing is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct thermodynamic integration on a selected high-entropy alloy system by running two sets of free-energy calculations: one using traditional EAM reference potentials (TOR-TILD) and one using DNN-based potentials. Both sets are to be performed across a temperature range spanning just below to above the melting point. Compare the integration path lengths, phase-space overlap metrics, and free energy estimates against high-accuracy ab initio benchmarks.
measurements: Thermodynamic integration path length (e.g., accumulated work along the integration path)
Phase-space overlap metrics (such as radial distribution functions and pair correlation comparisons)
Free energy differences computed for each method
Statistical error analysis of the free energy estimates relative to the ab initio benchmarks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DNN-based potentials do not show a statistically significant reduction in the thermodynamic-integration mismatch (i.e., no substantial improvement in phase-space overlap or free energy accuracy) compared to the traditional EAM approach, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.
